Description: A fungal infection is a skin condition caused by microscopic fungi that invade the outer layers of skin, nails, or hair. Common types include ringworm, athlete's foot, and nail fungus. They thrive in warm, moist environments and spread through direct contact.

Acne is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that occurs when hair follicles become clogged with oil and dead skin cells, leading to whiteheads, blackheads, pimples, and sometimes deeper lumps. It most commonly affects the face, chest, and back, and is particularly prevalent during adolescence.

Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune skin disorder that accelerates the life cycle of skin cells, causing them to build up rapidly on the surface and form scales and red patches that can be itchy and sometimes painful. It is a long-term condition with cycles of flaring and remission.

Impetigo is a highly contagious superficial bacterial skin infection caused primarily by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. It presents as red sores that quickly rupture, ooze, and form a yellowish-brown crust, most commonly affecting the face and extremities in young children.

An allergy is an exaggerated immune system response to a normally harmless substance called an allergen, such as pollen, pet dander, food, insect stings, or medications. The immune system produces antibodies that trigger symptoms ranging from mild sneezing and rashes to severe anaphylaxis.

A drug reaction is an unintended, harmful response to a medication taken at a normal dose. It can range from mild skin rashes and nausea to severe conditions like anaphylaxis or organ damage. Any medication can potentially cause a reaction, and severity depends on the drug, dose, and individual sensitivity.

Chickenpox is a highly contagious viral infection caused by the varicella-zoster virus, characterised by an itchy blister-like rash that first appears on the chest, back, and face before spreading across the body. It is generally mild in healthy children but can be severe in adults, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals.

Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that causes patches of skin to become itchy, dry, cracked, and inflamed. It is most common in children but can occur at any age, often flaring in response to triggers like soaps, detergents, stress, or allergens, and is frequently associated with asthma and hay fever.

Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that primarily affects the face, causing persistent redness, visible blood vessels, and sometimes acne-like bumps. It tends to flare with triggers like sun exposure, spicy food, alcohol, or stress, and while not curable, it can be managed with treatment.

Shingles is a viral infection caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus, which remains dormant in nerve tissue after a chickenpox infection. It produces a painful rash that usually appears as a stripe of blisters wrapping around one side of the torso, face, or neck, and can cause lasting nerve pain (postherpetic neuralgia).

Urticaria, commonly known as hives, is a skin reaction that causes raised, itchy, red or skin-coloured welts that can appear anywhere on the body. It is often triggered by an allergic reaction, infection, stress, or medication, and while most cases resolve within a few hours, chronic urticaria can persist for months or years.

Seborrheic dermatitis is a common chronic skin condition causing scaly patches, red skin, and stubborn dandruff, primarily affecting the scalp but also the oily areas of the face and body. It is thought to be related to a yeast that lives on skin and an inflammatory response, and tends to flare with stress or seasonal changes.

The common cold is a mild viral upper respiratory tract infection caused most often by rhinoviruses. It is the most frequently occurring illness in humans, presenting with a runny nose, sneezing, sore throat, and mild fever. Symptoms typically resolve within 7 to 10 days without specific treatment.

Influenza (flu) is a contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses that infect the nose, throat, and lungs. Unlike the common cold, flu typically has a sudden onset with high fever, severe body aches, fatigue, and chills. It can lead to serious complications including pneumonia, especially in older adults and young children.

Pneumonia is an acute infection that inflames the air sacs (alveoli) in one or both lungs, which may fill with fluid or pus. It can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi, and ranges in severity from mild to life-threatening. Bacterial pneumonia is the most common serious type in adults.

Bronchial asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways in which the airways narrow, swell, and may produce extra mucus, making breathing difficult. It causes recurring episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and coughing, triggered by allergens, exercise, cold air, or respiratory infections.

Tuberculosis (TB) is a serious infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis, primarily affecting the lungs but potentially spreading to other organs. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. A persistent cough, night sweats, and unexplained weight loss are hallmark symptoms.

COPD is a chronic inflammatory lung disease that causes obstructed airflow from the lungs, encompassing emphysema and chronic bronchitis. The primary cause is long-term exposure to cigarette smoke or other lung irritants. It is progressive and currently incurable, but treatment can control symptoms and slow progression.

Pleuritis (pleurisy) is an inflammation of the pleura — the two-layered membrane that surrounds the lungs and lines the chest cavity. It causes sharp chest pain that worsens during breathing, coughing, or sneezing. It can be caused by viral or bacterial infections, autoimmune diseases, or pulmonary embolism.

Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) is a chronic digestive disorder in which stomach acid or bile flows back into the oesophagus, irritating its lining. The most common symptom is heartburn — a burning sensation in the chest — along with regurgitation of sour liquid. Left untreated, GERD can lead to oesophageal damage.

Gastroenteritis is an inflammation of the stomach and intestines, most commonly caused by viral or bacterial infection through contaminated food or water, or contact with an infected person. It causes vomiting, diarrhoea, stomach cramps, and nausea, and usually resolves within a few days with rest and adequate hydration.

Peptic ulcer disease involves open sores (ulcers) that develop on the inner lining of the stomach, the upper portion of the small intestine, or the oesophagus. They are most commonly caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or long-term use of NSAIDs, producing burning stomach pain that is often worse on an empty stomach.

Chronic cholestasis is a condition where bile flow from the liver is reduced or blocked for a prolonged period, causing bile to build up in the liver rather than draining into the small intestine. This leads to intense itching, jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools, and can cause progressive liver damage over time.

Hemorrhoids (piles) are swollen and inflamed veins in the rectum and anus, similar to varicose veins. They can be internal (inside the rectum) or external (under the skin around the anus) and cause pain, itching, discomfort, and rectal bleeding. They are commonly caused by straining during bowel movements, chronic constipation, or pregnancy.

Acidity or hyperacidity is a condition in which the stomach produces excess hydrochloric acid beyond what is needed for digestion. This causes a burning sensation in the stomach and throat (heartburn), sour belching, nausea, and indigestion. It is often triggered by spicy food, stress, irregular eating habits, or certain medications like NSAIDs.

Loose motions or acute diarrhoea refers to frequent, watery, or loose bowel movements that occur suddenly and typically resolve within a few days. Common causes include bacterial or viral infections, contaminated food or water, food intolerances, or sudden dietary changes. Dehydration is the most important complication to manage.

Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is a common chronic gastrointestinal disorder that affects the large intestine, causing recurring abdominal pain, bloating, cramping, and altered bowel habits (diarrhoea, constipation, or both) without any structural damage. It is often triggered by stress, certain foods, and hormonal changes.

Appendicitis is an inflammation of the appendix — a small, finger-shaped pouch attached to the large intestine. It typically begins with pain near the navel that shifts to the lower right abdomen and becomes severe. If left untreated, the appendix can rupture, causing a life-threatening infection. It requires emergency surgical removal.

Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder in which ingestion of gluten — a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye — triggers an immune response that damages the lining of the small intestine, impairing the absorption of nutrients. Symptoms include diarrhoea, bloating, fatigue, and weight loss, and the only treatment is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet.

Chronic constipation is characterised by infrequent bowel movements (fewer than three per week), difficulty passing stools, or a persistent feeling of incomplete emptying lasting for several weeks or more. It can result from a low-fibre diet, inadequate fluid intake, physical inactivity, medications, or underlying conditions like IBS or thyroid disease.

Food poisoning is an illness caused by consuming food or beverages contaminated with bacteria (such as Salmonella or E. coli), viruses, parasites, or toxins. Symptoms typically begin within hours of eating the contaminated food and include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, stomach cramps, and fever. Most cases resolve within a few days without treatment.

Gallstones are hardened deposits of digestive fluid — mainly cholesterol or bilirubin — that form in the gallbladder. Many people have gallstones without symptoms, but when a stone blocks the bile duct, it causes sudden and intense pain in the upper right abdomen that may radiate to the back or right shoulder, accompanied by nausea and vomiting.

Lactose intolerance is the inability to fully digest lactose, the natural sugar found in milk and dairy products, due to insufficient production of the enzyme lactase in the small intestine. This causes digestive symptoms including bloating, diarrhoea, gas, and stomach cramps within 30 minutes to two hours of consuming dairy products.

Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas that can be acute (sudden and severe) or chronic (developing over many years). The most common causes are gallstones and heavy alcohol use. It presents with severe upper abdominal pain that often radiates to the back, nausea, vomiting, and fever. Severe cases can be life-threatening.

Jaundice is a yellowing of the skin, whites of the eyes, and mucous membranes caused by a build-up of bilirubin in the blood. It is not a disease itself but a sign of an underlying condition affecting the liver, bile ducts, or red blood cells, such as hepatitis, gallstones, or haemolytic anaemia.

Hepatitis A is a highly contagious acute liver infection caused by the hepatitis A virus, typically transmitted through contaminated food or water. It causes fever, fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, and jaundice. Unlike other forms of hepatitis, it does not cause chronic liver disease and most people recover fully within a few weeks.

Hepatitis B is a serious viral infection that attacks the liver and can cause both acute and chronic disease. It is transmitted through contact with infected blood, sexual contact, or from mother to child at birth. Chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer. A safe and effective vaccine is available for prevention.

Hepatitis C is a blood-borne viral infection that causes liver inflammation, silently progressing to serious liver damage in many people. It is primarily spread through contact with infected blood. Unlike Hepatitis A and B, there is no vaccine, but it is now curable with antiviral medications in most cases.

Hepatitis D is a serious liver disease caused by the hepatitis D virus, which only occurs in people already infected with hepatitis B — it requires the hepatitis B virus to replicate. It can cause acute or chronic infection and leads to more severe liver disease than hepatitis B alone. Prevention relies on hepatitis B vaccination.

Hepatitis E is a viral liver disease caused by the hepatitis E virus, primarily transmitted through contaminated drinking water. It causes acute liver infection with jaundice, fatigue, and nausea, and is usually self-limiting. However, it can be life-threatening in pregnant women, particularly during the third trimester.

Alcoholic hepatitis is an inflammatory condition of the liver caused by heavy, prolonged alcohol consumption. It ranges from mild to severe and life-threatening. Symptoms include jaundice, abdominal pain, swelling, nausea, vomiting, and confusion (encephalopathy). Severe cases carry a high short-term mortality risk.

Malaria is a life-threatening disease caused by Plasmodium parasites, transmitted through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. It is characterised by cycles of high fever, chills, and sweating, along with headache, muscle pain, and fatigue. If untreated, it can cause severe complications including organ failure and death.

Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection caused by the dengue virus, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. It presents with sudden high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, joint and muscle pain, rash, and nausea. A small proportion of cases progress to severe dengue, which can be fatal due to plasma leakage and bleeding.

Typhoid fever is a systemic bacterial infection caused by Salmonella typhi, transmitted through contaminated food and water. It presents with a prolonged high fever, weakness, stomach pain, headache, and loss of appetite. Without prompt antibiotic treatment, it can lead to serious intestinal complications.

AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome) is the most advanced stage of HIV infection, occurring when the immune system is severely damaged by the HIV virus. It leaves the body unable to fight infections and diseases that a healthy immune system would control. While there is no cure, antiretroviral therapy (ART) effectively controls HIV and prevents progression to AIDS.

Sepsis is a life-threatening medical emergency that occurs when the body's response to an infection becomes dysregulated and starts damaging its own tissues and organs. It can lead rapidly to septic shock, multi-organ failure, and death if not recognised and treated immediately with antibiotics and supportive care.

Cellulitis is a common and potentially serious bacterial skin infection that causes redness, swelling, warmth, and pain in the affected area, most often the lower legs. It occurs when bacteria — usually Staphylococcus or Streptococcus — enter through a break in the skin. It can spread rapidly and requires prompt antibiotic treatment.

Tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils — the two oval-shaped pads of tissue at the back of the throat — most commonly caused by viral or bacterial infection. It presents with a sore throat, swollen red tonsils, difficulty swallowing, fever, and swollen lymph nodes in the neck. Recurrent cases may require surgical removal (tonsillectomy).

Sinusitis is an inflammation of the sinuses — the hollow cavities around the nasal passages — usually caused by a viral infection following a cold, but also by bacteria or allergies. It causes facial pain and pressure, nasal congestion, thick nasal discharge, loss of smell, and headache. Chronic sinusitis lasts 12 weeks or more.

Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra — the tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body. It is commonly caused by bacterial infection, including sexually transmitted infections like gonorrhoea or chlamydia. Symptoms include a burning sensation during urination, discharge, and pelvic discomfort.

Otitis media is an infection of the middle ear — the space behind the eardrum — commonly caused by bacterial or viral infection, often following a cold or respiratory illness. It is especially common in children and causes ear pain, pressure, fluid drainage, hearing difficulty, and fever.

Conjunctivitis (pink eye) is an inflammation of the conjunctiva — the transparent membrane lining the eyelid and covering the white of the eye. It is caused by bacteria, viruses, or allergens, and results in redness, watery or thick discharge, itching, and a gritty feeling. The infectious form is highly contagious.

Mumps is a contagious viral infection caused by the mumps virus, characterised by painful swelling of the salivary glands — particularly the parotid glands — giving the face a puffy appearance. It also causes fever, headache, and muscle pain. It is preventable by the MMR vaccine and was once a major childhood illness.

Measles is a highly contagious viral infection caused by the measles virus, characterised by a high fever, cough, runny nose, red watery eyes, and a distinctive red skin rash that starts on the face and spreads downward. It is preventable by vaccination and can cause severe complications including pneumonia and encephalitis.

Polycystic Ovarian Disease (PCOD) is a hormonal condition in women in which the ovaries produce an abnormally large number of partially mature or immature eggs that eventually become cysts. It leads to irregular periods, hormonal imbalances, weight gain, and acne. PCOD is considered more manageable than PCOS and can often be improved through lifestyle changes.

Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is a complex hormonal endocrine disorder in women of reproductive age, characterised by elevated levels of androgens (male hormones), irregular or absent menstrual cycles, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. It is associated with insulin resistance, weight gain, infertility, and a higher long-term risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

Endometriosis is a chronic condition in which tissue similar to the uterine lining (endometrium) grows outside the uterus — on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, or pelvic lining. Each month this tissue behaves like normal endometrium — it thickens, breaks down, and bleeds — but has no way to exit the body, causing inflammation, severe pelvic pain, and scar tissue formation.

Menorrhagia is abnormally heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding — soaking through one or more sanitary pads or tampons per hour for several consecutive hours, or bleeding lasting more than 7 days. It can be caused by uterine fibroids, hormonal imbalances, polyps, or bleeding disorders, and often leads to iron-deficiency anaemia.

Dysmenorrhoea refers to painful menstrual cramps that occur just before or during a menstrual period. Primary dysmenorrhoea is common cramping not linked to another condition, caused by uterine contractions triggered by prostaglandins. Secondary dysmenorrhoea is pain caused by an underlying condition such as endometriosis or fibroids.

Preeclampsia is a serious pregnancy complication characterised by high blood pressure and signs of damage to another organ system — most often the liver or kidneys — occurring after 20 weeks of pregnancy. It can rapidly become life-threatening and requires close monitoring, blood pressure management, and in many cases early delivery of the baby.

Vaginitis is an inflammation of the vagina that can cause discharge, itching, and pain. The most common types are bacterial vaginosis (caused by bacterial overgrowth), yeast infections (caused by Candida), and trichomoniasis (a sexually transmitted infection). Each has distinct characteristics in terms of discharge type, odour, and treatment.

An ovarian cyst is a fluid-filled sac that develops on or inside an ovary. Most ovarian cysts form naturally during ovulation and resolve on their own without treatment. However, some cysts can grow large, rupture, or cause the ovary to twist (torsion), resulting in sudden severe pelvic pain that requires emergency medical attention.

A heart attack (myocardial infarction) occurs when blood flow to a section of the heart muscle becomes blocked — usually by a blood clot in a coronary artery — causing that section of muscle to begin dying from lack of oxygen. It is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment. Classic symptoms include chest pain, shortness of breath, and pain radiating to the left arm.

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is a chronic condition in which the force of blood against artery walls is consistently too high, defined as a reading of 140/90 mmHg or higher. It is often called the 'silent killer' because it frequently has no symptoms but significantly increases the risk of heart disease, stroke, and kidney failure.

Varicose veins are enlarged, twisted, and swollen veins that most commonly appear on the legs and feet. They occur when valves in the veins malfunction, causing blood to pool. While often a cosmetic concern, they can cause aching pain, swelling, heaviness, and in serious cases lead to skin ulcers or blood clots.

Angina is chest pain or discomfort that occurs when the heart muscle does not get enough oxygen-rich blood, usually due to narrowed coronary arteries. It is typically triggered by physical exertion or emotional stress and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. Angina is a warning sign of coronary artery disease and increases the risk of heart attack.

Atrial fibrillation (AFib) is the most common heart rhythm disorder, characterised by irregular and often rapid electrical impulses in the upper chambers of the heart (atria). This causes an irregular and sometimes fast heart rate, breathlessness, fatigue, and palpitations. It significantly increases the risk of stroke and heart failure.

Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) is the formation of a blood clot in a deep vein, typically in the legs. It causes leg pain, swelling, warmth, and redness. The most dangerous complication is a pulmonary embolism, which occurs if the clot breaks off and travels to the lungs. Risk factors include prolonged immobility, surgery, and pregnancy.

Diabetes mellitus is a group of chronic metabolic diseases characterised by elevated blood glucose levels resulting from defects in insulin production, insulin action, or both. Type 1 is an autoimmune condition; Type 2 is the most common form, linked to lifestyle and genetics. Long-term complications include damage to the heart, kidneys, eyes, and nerves.

Hypoglycaemia is a condition in which blood sugar (glucose) levels fall below the normal range, typically below 70 mg/dL. It most commonly occurs in people with diabetes as a side effect of insulin or certain diabetes medications, but can also occur in non-diabetics. Symptoms include shakiness, sweating, confusion, rapid heartbeat, and if severe, loss of consciousness.

Hypothyroidism is a condition in which the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone to meet the body's needs. Without adequate thyroid hormone, the body's metabolism slows down, causing symptoms such as fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, and depression. The most common cause is Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

Hyperthyroidism is a condition in which the thyroid gland produces too much of the hormone thyroxine, accelerating the body's metabolism. This can cause unintentional weight loss, rapid heartbeat, increased appetite, sweating, nervousness, and trembling. The most common cause is Graves' disease, an autoimmune disorder.

Anaemia is a condition in which the blood has a lower than normal number of healthy red blood cells, or the red blood cells lack sufficient haemoglobin, reducing the blood's ability to carry adequate oxygen to tissues. The most common cause is iron deficiency. Symptoms include fatigue, weakness, pale skin, breathlessness, and dizziness.

Obesity is a complex chronic condition defined by an excess accumulation of body fat — typically a Body Mass Index (BMI) of 30 or above — that significantly impairs health. It substantially increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, hypertension, certain cancers, sleep apnoea, and joint problems, and is caused by a combination of genetic, behavioural, and environmental factors.

Vitamin D deficiency occurs when the body does not get or absorb enough vitamin D, which is essential for bone health, immune function, and muscle function. It can result from inadequate sun exposure, poor dietary intake, or impaired absorption. It leads to weakened bones (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults), muscle weakness, fatigue, and mood changes.

Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide, occurring when the body's iron stores are depleted below the level needed to maintain normal physiological function. It is the most common cause of anaemia and results in fatigue, weakness, pale skin, brittle nails, shortness of breath, and impaired cognitive function.

Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluids than it takes in, disrupting normal bodily functions. It can result from excessive sweating, vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, or insufficient fluid intake. Mild dehydration causes thirst and dark urine; severe dehydration can cause confusion, rapid heartbeat, low blood pressure, and organ failure.

Heat stroke is a severe, life-threatening form of heat illness that occurs when the body's temperature regulation system fails and core body temperature rises to 40°C (104°F) or higher. It is characterised by hot dry skin, confusion, rapid heartbeat, and loss of consciousness. It constitutes a medical emergency requiring immediate cooling measures.

Arthritis is a broad term covering over 100 conditions that cause inflammation and pain in the joints. The most common forms are osteoarthritis (wear-and-tear) and rheumatoid arthritis (autoimmune). Symptoms include joint pain, stiffness, swelling, and reduced range of motion, and the condition can worsen progressively with age.

Osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis, caused by the gradual breakdown of cartilage — the protective cushion between bones — leading to pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility, particularly in the knees, hips, hands, and spine. It is most prevalent in older adults and is influenced by weight, joint injury, and genetics.

Cervical spondylosis is age-related wear and tear of the cervical spine (neck) involving degeneration of the vertebrae, discs, and joints. It is extremely common in people over 60 and can cause neck pain, stiffness, headaches, and in more severe cases, nerve compression leading to numbness or weakness in the arms and hands.

Gout is a form of inflammatory arthritis caused by the accumulation of uric acid crystals in a joint, typically the big toe. It causes sudden, severe attacks of pain, redness, swelling, and tenderness. It is associated with a high-purine diet, excess alcohol consumption, obesity, and kidney disease, and can become chronic if untreated.

Sciatica is pain that radiates along the path of the sciatic nerve — from the lower back through the hip, buttock, and down one leg. It is usually caused by a herniated disc, bone spur, or spinal stenosis compressing part of the nerve, and can cause numbness, tingling, and muscle weakness in the affected leg.

Fibromyalgia is a chronic disorder characterised by widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, sleep disturbances, and cognitive difficulties (often called 'fibro fog'). It is thought to involve amplified pain signalling in the brain and spinal cord, and is often triggered or worsened by stress, infection, physical trauma, or psychological distress.

Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) is a condition causing progressive stiffness and pain in the shoulder joint, resulting from thickening and tightening of the joint capsule. It typically progresses through three stages: freezing (increasing pain), frozen (decreased pain but persistent stiffness), and thawing (gradual improvement), lasting one to three years total.

Plantar fasciitis is one of the most common causes of heel pain, involving inflammation of the plantar fascia — the thick band of tissue connecting the heel bone to the toes. It causes stabbing pain that is typically worst with the first steps in the morning or after long periods of rest, and is common in runners, overweight individuals, and those who stand for long hours.

Migraine is a neurological disorder characterised by recurrent, severe headaches typically affecting one side of the head, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and extreme sensitivity to light and sound. Attacks can last from a few hours to several days and are often preceded by warning symptoms called an aura, such as visual disturbances.

Paralysis due to brain haemorrhage occurs when bleeding in the brain (haemorrhagic stroke) damages areas that control muscle movement, resulting in weakness or complete loss of function in one side of the body (hemiplegia). It is a medical emergency requiring immediate intervention. Early rehabilitation can help recover some function.

Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) is the most common cause of vertigo — the sudden sensation that you or your environment is spinning. It is caused by tiny calcium crystals in the inner ear becoming dislodged and moving into the wrong canal. It triggers brief but intense dizziness with head position changes and is treatable with specific repositioning manoeuvres.

Depression (Major Depressive Disorder) is a common and serious mental health condition causing persistent feelings of sadness, emptiness, hopelessness, and a loss of interest in activities once enjoyed. It affects how a person feels, thinks, and handles daily activities, and can cause both emotional and physical symptoms. It is highly treatable with therapy, medication, or a combination of both.

Anxiety disorders are a group of mental health conditions characterised by persistent, excessive fear or worry that is difficult to control and interferes with daily activities. They include Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD), panic disorder, social anxiety, and phobias. Physical symptoms such as rapid heartbeat, sweating, and muscle tension are common.

Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (CFS), also known as Myalgic Encephalomyelitis (ME), is a complex, long-term illness characterised by extreme fatigue that is not explained by any underlying medical condition and does not improve with rest. It is often worsened by physical or mental activity (post-exertional malaise), and may be accompanied by cognitive difficulties, sleep problems, and widespread pain.

Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder characterised by recurrent, unprovoked seizures — brief episodes of abnormal, excessive, or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain. Seizures can vary widely in type, from brief lapses of awareness to prolonged convulsions. It affects people of all ages and is managed primarily with antiseizure medications.

Insomnia is a common sleep disorder in which a person has persistent difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting restorative sleep, despite adequate opportunity to sleep. It can be short-term (acute) or long-term (chronic, lasting three months or more) and leads to daytime fatigue, mood disturbances, impaired concentration, and reduced quality of life.

Bipolar disorder is a serious mental health condition causing extreme mood swings that include emotional highs (mania or hypomania) and lows (depression). During manic episodes, a person may feel euphoric, full of energy, or unusually irritable; during depressive episodes, they feel hopeless and lose interest in activities. These mood shifts can affect sleep, judgment, behaviour, and relationships.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by persistent patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that are more frequent and severe than typically observed in individuals at a comparable level of development. It affects children and often continues into adulthood, impacting academic performance, work, and relationships.

A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection in any part of the urinary system — kidneys, ureters, bladder, or urethra — most commonly affecting the bladder and urethra. Caused primarily by bacteria (especially E. coli), UTIs are much more common in women and cause a burning sensation during urination, frequent urges to urinate, and cloudy or foul-smelling urine.

Kidney stones are hard mineral and salt deposits that form inside the kidneys when urine becomes concentrated and minerals crystallise. They can affect any part of the urinary tract and range from the size of a grain of sand to a golf ball. Passing a stone causes severe, sharp pain in the back and side, blood in urine, nausea, and vomiting.

Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is the gradual loss of kidney function over months or years. As the disease progresses, dangerous levels of fluid, electrolytes, and waste can build up in the body. In the early stages there may be no symptoms; later symptoms include fatigue, swelling, shortness of breath, and confusion. Diabetes and high blood pressure are the leading causes.

Prostatitis is inflammation of the prostate gland, which can be caused by bacterial infection (acute or chronic bacterial prostatitis) or by a non-infectious inflammatory condition. It causes pelvic pain, painful or difficult urination, pain during ejaculation, and in acute bacterial cases, fever and chills. It is the most common urological condition in men under 50.

Glaucoma is a group of eye conditions that damage the optic nerve — often due to abnormally high pressure in the eye — leading to gradual, irreversible vision loss. It is one of the leading causes of blindness worldwide. The most common form (open-angle glaucoma) has no symptoms in early stages, making regular eye exams critical for early detection.

A cataract is a clouding of the normally clear lens of the eye, which progressively blurs vision. It develops when proteins in the lens clump together and reduce the passage of light to the retina. Cataracts are most commonly age-related and cause blurry or dim vision, increased sensitivity to glare, faded colours, and poor night vision. Surgery is the only effective treatment.

Thyroid nodules are lumps that form within the thyroid gland, most of which are benign. However, a small percentage may be malignant (thyroid cancer). Early thyroid cancer is often discovered incidentally as a painless lump in the neck. Other potential signs include hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, swollen lymph nodes in the neck, and a persistent cough not due to infection.

Colorectal cancer is cancer that begins in the colon or rectum. In its early stages it may cause no symptoms, but warning signs include a persistent change in bowel habits, blood in or on the stool, persistent abdominal discomfort, a feeling that the bowel does not empty completely, unexplained weight loss, and fatigue. Regular screening is key to early detection when treatment is most effective.
